newsitem.title: USA: Senate investigators delve into China funds link.
newsitem.headline: Senate investigators delve into China funds link.

text.p: Republican investigators on Wednesday delved into Asian American John Huang's role in an alleged plan to raise foreign funds for Democrats as the party sought to build a case that its members acted within the law.

Senate Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Fred Thompson opened the second day of hearings on campaign finance abuses, again stressing his belief that China plotted to influence the U.S. political process and its foreign policy.
But the panel's first witness, Richard Sullivan, former finance director for the Democratic National Committee, said he never saw any evidence of a Chinese effort to tamper with the 1996 elections.

"That is, I was never -- I emphasise never -- confronted at the time with any evidence or suggestion of wilful misconduct, foreign government influence, sale of office, contributions in violation of the Federal Election Campaign Act or other legal problems of that kind," he said.

Republican Sen. Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania laid out a case that Chinese arms dealer Wang Jun was a link to China's government. Wang attended a February 1996 White House reception, a visit President Bill Clinton later said he regretted had occurred.

"The public record is clear that Wang Jun has a high tie to a very high-level Chinese official and that he's the head of a major arms dealer," Specter said, telling Sullivan DNC officials should have noticed "red flags all over the place."

Republicans questioned Sullivan extensively about the decision to hire Huang as a top Democratic fund raiser and the efforts by persons connected with the Indonesian Lippo Group who made calls and held meetings on Huang's behalf.

Huang is a former senior Commerce Department official in the area of international trade who had worked for Lippo, a real estate and financial conglomerate owned by the Riady family of Indonesia which has business interests in China.

Sullivan confirmed that former White House Chief of Staff Harold Ickes twice called DNC finance chairman Marvin Rosen to press for Huang's hiring. He also said James Riady had a meeting with DNC chairman Don Fowler at which Huang was present and that Little Rock, Arkansas, lawyer Joseph Giroir, who worked with Riady, tried to get Huang hired by the party.

While the DNC had reservations about Huang's lack of experience, he said in response to questions from Democrats that Huang was "most articulate" in his desire to help build support for Democrats in the Asian American community.

Huang raised $3.4 million for Democrats but about half that amount was returned as illegal or suspect. The committee's senior Democrat, Sen. John Glenn of Ohio, noted that only about 172 of more than two million contributions were returned.

Sullivan said there were reservations about Huang's fund raising and said he told Huang holding an official fund raiser in a Buddhist temple was against the law. The panel plans to call monks and nuns in its probe of $140,000 raised at the temple event attended by Vice President Al Gore.
Huang's lawyer, Ty Cobb, said on Tuesday his client will testify if given limited immunity from prosecution. This would protect him from charges of campaign finance violations.

Sullivan denied perks such as overnights in the White House Lincoln Bedroom or attendance at tapings of the president's weekly radio address were given to campaign high rollers. He vehemently denied that White House coffee meetings with donors were considered fund raisers although they were expected to "motivate and energise" attendees to help the party raise millions of dollars for the presidential campaign.

Senators of both parties decried the bending of campaign finance laws in the last elections but despite calls for reform no legislation is moving through Congress. The more than $600 million spent in the 1996 congressional and presidential campaigns -- nearly 50 percent more than the 1991-92 cycle -- broke all records.
